title: A thousand fewer paths to root (openai.com)
comments: How did we get to the point where there are a thousand privilege escalation exploits in the kernel?Is the kernel simply too complex to reason about? Is it an underlying flaw in the security model or language implementation?Should we assume that all software is more compromised than the kernel?reply

Because the large corporations that fund Linux development and use Linux value speed over security.Speed requires a lot of code in the kernel, where that code can run fast.There are kernels that do not have a thousand privilege escalation exploits. These kernels are smaller and much easier to check for bugs. But those kernels are significantly slower.For many use cases, slower is not a problem. But for the large corporations who fund a lot of Linux development and use Linux in large data centers, every 1% slower can literally be millions of dollars worth of additional servers that are required.OpenBSD shows that you can have a Unix security model without a thousand privilege escalation exploits. But OpenBSD is like 10% slower. So corporations won't use it because it would cost millions of dollars more per year and some of their software requires access that OpenBSD does not grant precisely because that access leads to security exploits (i.e. io_uring, eBPF etc. etc.)You could also use like seL4, but that's slow tooSo that's why. It's a business tradeoff between cost of servers vs cost of getting hacked, and cost of servers wins.reply
It also used to just be fine patching the bugs as they were found. Its only recently where that model has fallen apart and we now need to prevent the bugs from existing in the first place.reply

I'm pro OpenBSD, but the question to me seems: Has this been tested via the same means as these new Linux exploits?I'm also pretty hostile to AI, but do recognize that these machines seem to be very good at finding exploits.I'm sure there've been some some projects out there working to pentest/find cracks in OpenBSD via LLMs/agents/whatever-the-right-term-would-be...But it is true the attack surface is much lower in OpenBSD on purpose, so hopefully it is overall more secure. title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding (ricursive.com)
comments: Category narrowing to this degree really has diluted the term "SOTA" quite a lotYou mean it's state of the art for this subset of benchmarks you're targeting? No? Well surely it's state of the art for models of a certain size category? Huh, what about models that are available for local inference? O, state of the art for open models of a certain size made in the US specifically. Uh. Neat!reply

Playing games like this also makes it very easy to accidentally say things that aren't true, like in the headline of the article...> Introducing Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight ModelIt's not "frontier", it's not "frontier" even in the category of open-weight models (though usually that phrasing would mean frontier over all, and also open weight)... it's only "frontier" in the small sub-category of US made open-weight models.reply

It is technically frontier, if by "frontier" we mean the Pareto frontier.Being at the Pareto frontier means that you can't get something better on one aspect without compromising on some other aspect. The trick is that it is easy to be at the Pareto frontier by having enough dimensions.Here, we have 4: score, number of parameters, origin (US) and open-weight. You can get a better score or a lower number of parameters, but you have to compromise on at least one of the other aspects. That's a pretty weak frontier if you ask me.reply

“Origin” isn’t part of the Pareto frontier because it’s not a quantitative dimension.(You could say that “ability to be trusted by US government/military users” is quantifiable, but I would argue that by that metric, this model falls behind non-US-originated open-weight models that have more eyes on them!)reply

Discrete dimensions can exist in Pareto considerations. Not that I'm too fond of this game, but given that "Origin" is definitely part of the calculus of model deployment, it makes sense to consider it in a Pareto calculation.reply

It's just a different pareto frontier because you're filtering out items that don't fit your criteria. "Model was made by Anthropic" would be an equivalent dimension. You would never plot this, you're just reducing the subset of models you're comparing.By that logic, any model is a frontier model. My GPT-2 clone is a frontier model when you compare it against models that were trained on my homelab.reply
Which you're welcome to do and then people are welcome to disagree that is an important frontier to consider.reply
Ahh I run into this issue all the time with ai when applying any sort of dimensional reasoning abstractly it always implicits continuousreply

AFAIK the currently biggest US open-weight model is Inkling, which they include in the comparison, so at least their claim is not limited to a size category. Still they score 0.42 percentage points higher than the second-best model on their chosen benchmark, so it's hardly a meaningful lead.reply

This reminds me of how I used to cheat at certain games back in the 8-bit olden days. You could change one thing at a time, save, then look through and see what changed on the disk. Eventually you could identify all the locations that held the values for inventory, stats, location, quest stages, NPC state, and so on. All you had to do after that was change those locations and - hopefully - you're all powered up. With the WozMon you could even find the locations in memory, sometimes, and have "free" healing spells, for instance, any time you like by popping open the monitor and just changing the values in RAM. Among people my age this is the usual way you'd get started with something resembling hacking. It seems like the author is doing the same type of thing. This is also the basis of cheats and trainers for games, action games tended to be easier and there might only be a handful of flags and variables making cheat menus practical. For RPGs the cheats came in the form of lists of locations on the disk, eventually though there were disk-based full blown character editors available for some handful of games. Also about the same time, some developers started to go to extreme lengths to keep people from cheating by tampering with their save game files. This became quite common in the industry by the 32-bit era.EDIT: I will point out that people would often submit letters to computer magazines with the memory locations of popular games as time went on. But this could take months or a year or more, and a game might never have its secrets laid bare so I suspect a LOT of people just did it manually at home.reply
